passage:
Friday. Suraj's teacher asked for a school model by the next Friday. He had no idea what to make, so instead of choosing, he opened the cupboard.
Saturday. On the balcony floor he laid out flat cardboard, bottle caps, a handful of ice-cream sticks and a coil of old wire. "Caps are wheels," said his brother Kunal. Suraj picked up the sticks and wire. "And these are a bridge." He began building a truck crossing a bridge.
Next Thursday. The model stood on his desk, bottle-cap wheels turning. The idea had come from the pile.

qa.q: What materials did Suraj lay out on the balcony?
qa.a: He laid out flat cardboard, bottle caps, ice-cream sticks and old wire.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling on Friday when he had no idea what to make?
qa.a: Unsure and stuck, which is why he opened the cupboard instead of choosing.

qa.q: What could Suraj try if the pile suggests nothing, and why?
qa.a: He could sketch a few rough ideas or ask Kunal for one, so there is a starting point to match with the materials.

qa.q: How might Kunal see the pile of materials?
qa.a: Kunal spots wheels in the bottle caps straight away, so he sees possibilities quickly and helps the idea along.

passage: Parveen, you're stuck because you decided on a volcano before looking in the cupboard. Let me tell you what I, Gautam, did in Class 5. Our teacher said, "Any model, due Monday." Everyone rushed to buy kits. We had no money for kits. So I tipped the junk box from under the bed onto the floor: a flattened cardboard carton, twelve bottle caps, a bundle of ice-cream sticks, and a coil of old wire from a broken radio. I sat and looked. The caps were round. Wheels? The sticks were straight. A frame? The wire could bend into an axle. By evening it wasn't a volcano or a rocket. It was a little cart that actually rolled. Your Dadi still has it somewhere.

qa.q: What did Gautam find in the junk box?
qa.a: A flattened cardboard carton, twelve bottle caps, a bundle of ice-cream sticks and a coil of old wire.

qa.q: What was young Gautam thinking as he sat and looked at the pile?
qa.a: Young Gautam felt curious, letting the shapes suggest uses: round caps as wheels, straight sticks as a frame.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the difference?
qa.a: Emptying the junk box and looking before deciding what to build, so the materials shaped the idea.

qa.q: How might Gautam's mother have felt about the cart?
qa.a: She has kept it all these years, which suggests she was proud of it.

grounding: An elder recalls letting the scraps at home suggest what to build for a school model.

passage: The shops were shut because of a strike, and Ramesh's model for Science Day was due in the morning. His plan had been a solar system with foam balls. No foam balls. His sister Devika found him staring at the empty table. "Stop wanting what you can't get," she said, and tipped the recycling bag onto the floor. Ramesh knelt. Two toothpaste boxes, a handful of straws, rubber bands, a torn slipper, an empty milk packet. He turned the straws in his fingers. "Straws are pipes," he muttered. "Boxes are tanks." The slipper's rubber could be cut into a flap. By ten at night he had a model of a village water tank with pipes, and water ran through when he squeezed the milk packet.

qa.q: What was Ramesh thinking as he turned the straws in his fingers?
qa.a: He was curious and hopeful, starting to see the straws as pipes and the boxes as tanks.

qa.q: What else could Ramesh have done if the recycling bag had been nearly empty?
qa.a: He could have asked neighbours for scraps or told the teacher and brought a simpler model, since a small working idea beats nothing.

qa.q: How might Devika see the finished tank?
qa.a: She pushed him to look at what he had, so she would likely feel pleased and a little proud.

grounding: Under a deadline with shops closed, a boy looks at the scraps at home and lets them suggest a new model.
